items.statement: Some people believe that secondary school pupils should study only the subjects in which they already perform well, rather than following a broad curriculum.
items.instruction: Do you agree or disagree?

body: main reason for the chosen side

pro: Early specialisation lets pupils develop real depth in their strongest subjects.
A lighter timetable leaves more time for practice and reduces exam stress.
Universities and employers select candidates on proven strengths rather than broad but shallow knowledge.
con: Most teenagers do not yet know where their long-term strengths lie.
A narrow curriculum can leave gaps in literacy, numeracy and general knowledge.
Pupils who specialise and later change direction have few transferable skills.

referenceAnswers.text:
Many secondary schools allow pupils to choose a small number of subjects. Some people think that teenagers should focus only in the subjects where they get good marks. I agree with this idea because it helps pupils to become strong in one area.

Firstly, specialising early lets pupils develop real depth in their best subjects. When a student studies fewer subjects, he or she can spend more time on the ones that matter for the future. For example, a pupil who is good at chemistry can do more experiments and read more books about science, and this can help them to get a place at a good university. Also, a lighter timetable means less exam stress, so pupils are more happy and healthy. This gives them time for sport and other activities that keep them fit.

Secondly, universities and employers look at proven strengths, not broad but shallow knowledge. A student with excellent results in three subjects is usually more attractive than one with average results in eight. In addition, pupils who are weak in some subjects often feel unhappy in those lessons, and this can affect their confidence. They may stop trying in class and even begin to dislike school completely. If they study only their best subjects, they can enjoy school more, get better marks and feel more confident about the future. This confidence is important for their later life.

In conclusion, I agree that secondary pupils should study mainly the subjects in which they do well, because this gives them more time to practise and less stress from exams. This is the main reason for my opinion.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Your position is clear and relevant, but the support in "For example, a pupil who is good at chemistry can do more experiments and read more books about science" is thin - add a consequence so the example shows why depth matters.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Extend the example with a result: "...and this can lift their final grade, which universities weigh heavily."

referenceAnswers.text:
Many education systems ask teenagers to choose a few subjects to study in depth. Some people argue that this narrow focus should begin early, while others prefer a broad curriculum. In my opinion, specialisation is valuable, but only after pupils have completed a common core of general subjects.

The main benefit of later specialisation is that most teenagers are still discovering their strengths. A fifteen-year-old may enjoy biology this year and discover an aptitude for economics the next, so an early choice can close doors that should remain open. Delaying the decision by two or three years gives pupils time to test their interests and to build the literacy and numeracy that every career requires. They also become better judges of their own abilities. Consequently, the subjects they finally choose are more likely to match their real abilities and long-term goals.

A common core also protects pupils whose talents emerge late. Schools cannot predict which child will flourish in a subject at university, and a narrow timetable may leave a late developer without the foundation to switch direction. By contrast, pupils who continue with a broad curriculum until sixteen can change course without losing a year. A student who discovers an interest in law at seventeen, for instance, can still choose the subjects that lead to it. This flexibility matters in a labour market where careers and technologies change quickly, because adaptable learners cope better with such shifts.

In conclusion, I support specialisation in the final years of secondary school rather than at the start, since pupils need time to discover their strengths and a broad base keeps their options open when their plans change.
referenceAnswers.whyBand: Band 7 profile. The position is clear in the introduction, supported in both bodies and restated at the end. Ideas are extended with reasons and consequences, linkers vary (Consequently, By contrast), and some less common vocabulary appears (aptitude, literacy and numeracy, adaptable learners). A few minor slips remain, such as the loose connection in "which child will flourish in a subject at university", so the essay stops short of band 8.

evidenceSpan.text: By contrast, pupils who continue with a broad curriculum until sixteen can change course without losing a year.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Clear progression overall; strengthen the link in "By contrast, pupils who continue with a broad curriculum until sixteen can change course without losing a year" by naming what is being contrasted so the shift between the two sides is unmistakable.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Use a content-based signpost: "A broad timetable, by contrast, allows pupils to change direction without losing a year."

referenceAnswers.text:
Secondary schooling has traditionally balanced breadth with depth, yet some now argue that pupils should drop broad study and concentrate only on their strongest subjects. I disagree with that absolute position. A slim core should remain compulsory, while the rest of the timetable can be devoted to proven strengths.

Concentration unquestionably produces depth. A pupil who spends six hours a week on music rather than two advances far faster. Technique improves, repertoire grows, and the confidence gained in one field tends to spill over into others. Practice in one demanding subject also teaches habits of application that transfer elsewhere. Universities, too, select on evidence of sustained commitment, and a portfolio of graded performances or laboratory projects demonstrates that commitment far more convincingly than a string of average results across ten subjects. Where a school can timetable this depth without abandoning essentials, the gain is real rather than merely theoretical.

The difficulty lies in the word "only". Literacy, numeracy and a working knowledge of science are prerequisites for almost every career and for informed citizenship. A pupil who specialises at eleven and later changes direction may lack the very foundations needed to retrain. A teenager's stated strengths are also unstable, since interests harden only after exposure to a range of disciplines. Retaining a small compulsory core until sixteen therefore costs little and prevents expensive mistakes. Such a compromise preserves the benefits of depth while limiting the risk of a narrow education.

In conclusion, although specialising in proven strengths is beneficial, I cannot support an exclusively narrow curriculum. A compact core of general subjects should remain until pupils are old enough to choose wisely and to understand the consequences.
referenceAnswers.whyBand: Band 8 profile. The position is quantified and held throughout, and both bodies develop a mechanism, a consequence and an illustration before tying back to the question. Cohesion is managed through referencing and contrast rather than memorised linkers, and the range is wide and mostly precise (sustained commitment, prerequisites, unstable). It falls short of band 9 because the counter-argument is compressed into a single body rather than fully explored.

evidenceSpan.text: Universities, too, select on evidence of sustained commitment, and a portfolio of graded performances or laboratory projects demonstrates that commitment far more convincingly than a string of average results across ten subjects.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Precise vocabulary; the sentence "Universities, too, select on evidence of sustained commitment, and a portfolio of graded performances or laboratory projects demonstrates that commitment far more convincingly than a string of average results across ten subjects" repeats "commitment" and could carry a sharper contrast with a more exact term.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Replace the second mention with "such dedication" and vary "average results" to "undistinguished grades" to tighten the lexical chain.

referenceAnswers.text:
Museums and galleries in many countries receive money from the government. Some people think that these public museums should show only art from their own country. I agree with this view because public money should support local culture, and local art is often ignored.

Firstly, public money should display the nation's own story and heritage. Every country has its own history, and museums are the best place to show this to citizens and visitors. For example, a national gallery can show paintings about important events in the country's past, and this helps young people to understand where they come from and what their traditions mean. In addition, showing local art gives artists in the country more chances to become famous, and this support is important because many of them cannot find buyers without the help from public exhibitions.

Secondly, visitors come to a country to see its own culture, not a copy of a global collection. Tourists can see international art in their own cities or in the internet, but they cannot see local traditions anywhere else. Moreover, national collections are usually built from gifts and loans, so the works in them already belong to the country's story. If galleries mix everything together, the national character can become less clear, so a clear national focus makes a museum more special for everyone. In this way, the gallery also attracts more visitors, which brings income to the city.

In conclusion, I agree that publicly funded museums and galleries should mainly show works by artists from their own country, because this supports local culture and gives visitors something that they cannot see anywhere else in the world.

evidenceSpan.text: Tourists can see international art in their own cities or in the internet, but they cannot see local traditions anywhere else.

feedback.feedbackStarter: A mix of simple and complex structures, but the preposition in "Tourists can see international art in their own cities or in the internet, but they cannot see local traditions anywhere else" is wrong and pulls the accuracy score down.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Correct "in the internet" to "on the internet" and check other prepositions in the same paragraph ("the help from public exhibitions" -> "help from public exhibitions").

referenceAnswers.text:
National galleries depend on public funding, and some argue that this money should be spent only on domestic art. I disagree, although a country's own artists deserve a fair share of exhibition space. In my view, a mixed programme serves both citizens and artists better than an exclusively national one.

International works give citizens access to world culture without the cost of travelling. A school group in a small city can study Dutch painting or West African sculpture in the same afternoon, and such encounters widen both knowledge and taste. Publicly funded collections exist precisely because private markets would not provide this breadth. Restricting them to national work would make cultural education a privilege of those who can afford flights and hotels. In that sense, an open collection is a civic service rather than a luxury, and it allows residents to see how their own traditions fit into a wider history.

Exchange between countries also keeps art innovative rather than narrow. Artists learn from one another across borders, and a gallery that shows only domestic work isolates the very talent it claims to protect. Admittedly, local artists need support, and free exhibition space can provide it. However, that support need not exclude foreign loans. National work can hold a prominent place while international exhibitions rotate through the same rooms. This approach keeps audiences returning and gives local artists an international context in which to be judged. Visitors who come for a foreign exhibition often return for a domestic one, so both gain an audience.

In conclusion, while domestic artists merit firm public support, I disagree that publicly funded museums should show only national work, because access to world art and creative exchange benefit citizens and artists alike.
referenceAnswers.whyBand: Band 7 profile. The position is stated directly and maintained, and each body extends one idea with reasons and implications rather than listing points. Linkers are varied (Admittedly, However, In that sense), and there is some less common vocabulary (civic service, exclusively, rotate). A few minor slips and one slightly cliched phrase (a balance can be struck) keep it below band 8.

evidenceSpan.text: Admittedly, local artists need support, and free exhibition space can provide it. However, that support need not exclude foreign loans.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Your position is clear throughout; strengthen "Admittedly, local artists need support, and free exhibition space can provide it. However, that support need not exclude foreign loans" by explaining what local artists actually gain from a mixed programme.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Add one concrete benefit, for example: "...foreign loans draw visitors who then encounter domestic work in the same building."

referenceAnswers.text:
What publicly funded galleries display touches on cultural identity and taste, and some argue that national collections should be exclusively domestic. I partly agree. Flagship museums should give most of their space to home-grown work, yet a complete ban on foreign art would impoverish the audiences they serve.

There is a strong case for prioritising national work. Public money should make visible what private commerce overlooks, and a country's own artistic traditions are rarely lucrative enough to survive on ticket sales alone. When a national gallery devotes its principal rooms to domestic painting, sculpture or craft, it gives local artists both income and standing, and it offers visitors a narrative that no imported blockbuster can supply. Heritage, in this sense, is a public good that markets under-provide. A guaranteed majority of floor space is therefore a reasonable use of tax revenue.

That argument, however, does not justify a total ban. Art develops through contact, and galleries that seal themselves off from foreign influence tend to stagnate. The Impressionists learned from Japanese prints, and contemporary studios borrow freely across borders. Exchange also protects the public's education, since citizens who never encounter another culture abroad may never encounter it at all. A collection that closes its doors to foreign work narrows public taste. A quota of roughly two-thirds national work would preserve identity while keeping the collection alive. On that basis, I would defend a strong national bias but not an exclusive one.

In conclusion, I agree that publicly funded galleries should give priority to their own country's artists, but I cannot support an outright ban, because exposure to international work is what keeps a national tradition vital.
referenceAnswers.whyBand: Band 8 profile. A quantified partial position is stated in the introduction and developed through both bodies, with mechanisms (markets under-provide heritage; art develops through contact) and a specific proposal (a two-thirds quota). Cohesion is handled through referencing and content-based transitions, and the lexis is wide and mostly precise. One idea, the education argument, could be extended further, which is why the response sits at band 8 rather than 9.

evidenceSpan.text: Exchange also protects the public's education, since citizens who never encounter another culture abroad may never encounter it at all.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Your response is well developed; push the counter-argument in "Exchange also protects the public's education, since citizens who never encounter another culture abroad may never encounter it at all" one step further to show what is lost when a collection closes.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Add the consequence: "Without such encounters, public taste narrows and support for the arts itself may decline."

referenceAnswers.text:
Governments spend a lot of money on hospitals and doctors. Some people believe that this money should go to preventing illness instead of treating people who are already sick. I agree with this idea because prevention is cheaper and helps more people.

Firstly, preventing disease is much cheaper than treating it. Vaccination, clean water and regular health checks can protect a large number of people at a low cost, while the treatment of a serious illness can continue for many years. For example, a patient with heart disease may need medicine, surgery and hospital care for the rest of their life. If the government spends more on healthy eating campaigns and exercise programmes, fewer people will become sick in the first place. This means less sick people in the future and a smaller bill for the health service.

Secondly, prevention helps to reduce the pressure on hospitals. When fewer people suffer from preventable diseases, doctors and nurses have more time for patients which really need emergency care. In addition, healthy citizens can work and study better, so the whole country benefits. People who stay healthy also need fewer days off work, which helps businesses and the economy. However, some people say that patients who are ill now cannot wait for prevention to work, and this is a fair point. For this reason, the government should still keep enough money for treatment while it invests more in prevention.

In conclusion, I agree that the most of the public health budget should go to prevention, because it is cheaper and it reduces the number of sick people. This is the best way to protect the health of everyone.

referenceAnswers.text:
Health budgets are limited, and governments must decide how much to spend on preventing disease and how much on treating patients who are already ill. Some argue that prevention deserves the larger share. I largely agree, although emergency and cancer care must remain fully funded.

Prevention offers the better return on public money. Vaccination, clean water and screening programmes protect whole populations at a fraction of the cost of treating advanced disease, and they benefit people who would never seek help until their condition became serious. A patient who needs dialysis three times a week, for instance, consumes far more resources than a campaign that encourages early testing. Shifting part of the budget towards prevention therefore saves lives and money at the same time, and it reaches groups who rarely visit a doctor. Such programmes also reduce health inequalities, because the poorest families often gain the most from them.

This shift should not be allowed to weaken treatment. Patients who are ill now cannot wait for prevention to show results, and cutting emergency services would harm the elderly and the poorest first. The sensible approach is to increase prevention spending gradually, funded by savings elsewhere in the health system rather than by closing wards. Prevention campaigns must also reach the people most at risk, since advice about diet and exercise often appeals to those who are already healthy. Targeted outreach, not general advertising, is what changes behaviour. A balanced budget can pursue both goals at once.

In conclusion, I agree that prevention deserves a larger share of health budgets, but only if emergency and specialist treatment remain secure, because a fair system needs both approaches working together over the long term.
referenceAnswers.whyBand: Band 7 profile. A clear partial position is stated in the introduction, supported in both bodies and restated at the end. The ideas are extended rather than listed, and the second body handles the counter-argument while keeping the position intact. Linkers are flexible (Critically, therefore, by contrast) and some less common vocabulary appears (return on public money, screening programmes, acute). A few minor slips and one slightly vague sentence keep it below band 8.

evidenceSpan.text: This shift should not be allowed to weaken treatment.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Clear progression overall; the opener in "This shift should not be allowed to weaken treatment" is doing structural work, but the paragraph would read more naturally if the contrast were carried by content rather than announced so plainly.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Replace the opener with a content-based signpost: "Yet prevention cannot be funded by weakening treatment, because..."

referenceAnswers.text:
Public health budgets are finite, and money directed towards prevention is money not spent at a hospital bedside. Some argue that prevention should now take priority. I agree, provided that the shift is gradual and that acute care is protected, because the scale of preventable illness is too large to ignore.

The case for prevention rests on both cost and scale. Vaccination, clean water, tobacco control and screening reduce the burden of disease across an entire population, whereas treatment benefits one patient at a time. Chronic conditions such as diabetes and heart disease consume years of medication, surgery and hospital beds, yet many of them are largely avoidable through diet, exercise and early detection. Money invested in these measures therefore multiplies its effect, protecting people who never appear in hospital statistics at all. That is an argument about fairness as much as finance. It also reduces the pressure that preventable illness places on families and employers.

The argument has limits, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Someone injured in a road accident, or diagnosed with a cancer that no lifestyle choice could have prevented, needs immediate and expensive care, and a system that neglects such patients has failed them. The practical answer is to expand prevention without cutting emergency provision, using savings from reduced hospital admissions over time. Prevention campaigns must also be aimed at deprived communities, where disease rates are highest and where advice about healthy living is least likely to arrive.

In conclusion, I agree that prevention should receive a larger share of public health funding, since it protects more people at lower cost, but only alongside guaranteed treatment for those already ill.
referenceAnswers.whyBand: Band 8 profile. The position is nuanced and explicit, and each body develops a mechanism (population-level protection versus one-patient-at-a-time treatment) before conceding its limits. Cohesion is managed through referencing and contrast rather than listed linkers, and the lexis is wide and precise (avoidable, acute care, deprived communities). It stops short of band 9 because the funding mechanism for the transition is asserted rather than demonstrated.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Your position is well developed; the funding claim in "The practical answer is to expand prevention without cutting emergency provision, using savings from reduced hospital admissions over time" would be more convincing if you showed when those savings appear.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Add a time frame and a condition: "...once screening reduces admissions, which typically takes several years to show in hospital budgets."

Some people think that pupils should focus early on the subjects they are best at, while others believe that a broad education is more valuable. I agree with the first group to a small extent, but I think most pupils need a wide range of subjects.

Firstly, early specialisation can help talented pupils to progress faster. A student who is very good at mathematics can study advanced topics instead of repeating easy work, and this keeps them interested in school. In addition, a lighter timetable means less exam pressure, and pupils have more time to practise their best subject. For example, a young musician or athlete can train for many hours each week and reach a high level before the age of eighteen. This is a real benefit for children with a clear talent.

Secondly, however, most teenagers do not know what they want to do in the future. A pupil of fourteen may enjoy biology now but choose a career in business later, and a narrow education can leave them without the skills to change direction. Moreover, basic knowledge of languages, history and science helps people to understand the world and to make good decisions as citizens. Schools cannot predict which subject will be useful in twenty years, so they should teach a wide range of them. This also gives pupils more time to discover what they are really good at.

In conclusion, I agree only to a small extent that pupils should specialise early, because a few talented children benefit, but most teenagers need a broad education to keep their future options open and to prepare for a changing job market.

referenceAnswers.text:
Debate about the school curriculum often divides those who favour early specialisation and those who defend breadth. In my view, a broad education is more valuable for the majority of pupils, although specialisation should begin in the final years of secondary school for those with clear goals and strong academic records.

Breadth keeps options open in a labour market that changes quickly. Careers that seemed secure a generation ago have been transformed by automation, and workers who can combine skills from several fields adapt more easily than those trained for a single narrow role. A pupil who studies languages, mathematics and a science, for instance, can move into journalism, engineering or teaching without retraining from scratch. Early specialisation, by contrast, locks in a decision made before the pupil understands the working world at all. A choice made at fourteen is therefore a choice made in the dark.

Breadth also has a public value that is easy to overlook. Democratic societies depend on citizens who can evaluate scientific claims, follow economic arguments and understand other cultures, and these abilities are built at school across many subjects. Admittedly, gifted young musicians and athletes need intensive training early, and schools should accommodate them. However, such cases are exceptions, and designing the whole curriculum around them would leave most pupils with gaps that are difficult to fill later. A broad curriculum also gives every pupil a shared body of knowledge to discuss and debate.

In conclusion, I consider a broad education more valuable for most pupils, with early specialisation reserved for the final school years and for those who have exceptional talent and clear goals.

Linkers are varied (by contrast, Admittedly, However) and there is some less common vocabulary (automation, retraining from scratch, accommodate). A few minor slips and a slightly over-generalised claim about automation keep it below band 8.

evidenceSpan.text: Careers that seemed secure a generation ago have been transformed by automation

feedback.feedbackStarter: Main ideas are extended, but "Careers that seemed secure a generation ago have been transformed by automation" over-generalises; the claim needs a limiting phrase so it reads as a trend rather than a universal law.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Qualify the statement: "Many careers that seemed secure a generation ago have been reshaped by automation, particularly in manufacturing and administration."

referenceAnswers.text:
Few questions shape a young person's future more than how early the curriculum should narrow. Some argue that pupils should concentrate on their strongest subjects from the start. I largely disagree. Breadth is the more valuable foundation, and genuine depth is best pursued at university or in specialist training after school.

A broad curriculum builds the transferable capacities that a changing economy rewards. Reading critically, reasoning with numbers, writing clearly and understanding how societies work are not tied to any single occupation, yet they underpin almost all of them. A pupil who has studied history and statistics can move into market research, law or public administration, whereas one trained only in a technical specialism may struggle when that specialism is automated. Breadth, in other words, is insurance against an unpredictable future, and it is precisely the pupils who specialise earliest who have the least protection.

There is also a civic dimension. The counter-argument is that exceptional performers need many hours of practice while they are young, and this is true for elite musicians and athletes. Such pupils deserve flexibility, but they are a small minority, and their needs should not define the curriculum for everyone else. For the rest, breadth remains the safer and richer preparation.

In conclusion, I disagree with early specialisation for most pupils. A broad curriculum develops adaptable skills and informed citizens, and depth can safely follow once students know their direction and have the foundations to pursue it.

Many people believe that hard work is the only way to become successful at work. Others think that family background and luck are more important. In my opinion, hard work is the most important factor, although luck can help sometimes. I also believe that effort is more reliable than luck.

Firstly, hard work builds the skills and experience that employers want. People who work long hours and try to improve themselves learn faster than people which do not make an effort. For example, an employee who takes extra training and finishes every task on time is more likely to get a promotion. In addition, hard work creates a good reputation, and other companies may offer a better job to someone who is known for being reliable. This kind of employee is also less likely to be replaced when the company has to reduce its staff.

Secondly, hard work is something that a person can control, unlike luck or family connections. Nobody can choose to be born into a rich family, but everybody can choose to study, practise and work harder. However, some people are more lucky than others and lose their jobs when a company closes, and in this situation effort is not enough. Even so, workers who keep trying usually find another opportunity, because employers value people who do not give up. In most cases, the person who keeps applying for jobs and improving their skills will succeed in the end.

In conclusion, I believe that hard work is the main reason for career success, because it creates skills and opportunities. Luck and background can help, but they are less important. Young people should therefore be encouraged to work hard.

referenceAnswers.text:
Career success is often explained as the reward for effort, and some go further, claiming that only hard work matters whatever a person's background or luck may be. I agree that effort is essential, but I believe it is not sufficient on its own, because opportunities and connections also shape outcomes.

Effort remains the factor that individuals can most directly control. Skills are built through repetition, and reputations are built through reliability, so an employee who volunteers for difficult projects and masters new software steadily becomes more valuable. Over time, this record opens doors that would otherwise stay closed, since managers tend to promote people whose work they can trust. For most workers, sustained effort is the only lever they possess, and it is a powerful one. By contrast, a worker who avoids responsibility rarely develops the judgement that senior roles require.

Yet effort alone does not guarantee advancement. Family wealth, university networks and sheer timing can determine who is considered for the best roles, and a talented worker in a declining industry may struggle despite working harder than a competitor in a booming one. Automation can also remove skilled jobs regardless of dedication. The reasonable conclusion is that hard work improves a person's chances substantially but cannot be treated as the only ingredient of success. The fairest response is to reward effort while widening access to the training and networks that make effort count.

In conclusion, I believe that hard work is essential for career success, but background, timing and luck also play a part, so effort should be rewarded and obstacles acknowledged rather than ignored by employers and governments alike.

feedback.feedbackStarter: Main ideas are extended, but "Automation can also remove skilled jobs regardless of dedication" over-generalises; the claim needs a qualifier so it reads as a risk rather than a certainty.
feedback.fixSuggestion: Qualify it: "Automation can eliminate skilled roles in sectors such as manufacturing, however dedicated the workforce may be."

referenceAnswers.text:
The idea that only hard work produces career success is attractive because it promises that effort will always be rewarded. In my view it is misleading. Diligence is necessary, but background, opportunity and timing decide how far it can carry a person.

Hard work undeniably matters, and its effects are easiest to see in stable, meritocratic settings. A junior accountant who masters new software, takes on unpopular assignments and delivers reliably will usually advance faster than a colleague of similar ability who does the minimum. Employers reward demonstrated competence because it reduces their own risk when they choose whom to promote. That is why firms compete for staff with a record of delivery. Effort, in short, is the one variable the worker controls. Within those limits, effort is the most reliable investment a worker can make in his or her own future.

Those limits, however, are far tighter than the saying admits. A student from a wealthy family inherits professional contacts, unpaid internships and the security to wait for a good opening, advantages that no amount of evening study can fully offset. Economic downturns, industry closures and illness can erase years of effort through no fault of the worker. Meanwhile, others succeed through inheritance or simple timing. It is telling that many successful people combine ability with advantages they did not earn. Rewarding effort is sensible, but claiming that it alone determines success ignores how unevenly opportunity is distributed.

In conclusion, I disagree that only hard work leads to success. Effort is indispensable, yet it operates within circumstances that no individual fully controls. Public policy should therefore widen opportunity rather than simply praise effort.

Rich countries often send money and food to poorer countries. Some people argue that this aid should continue even when the rich country has economic problems. I agree with this idea, but I think the aid should be carefully checked and should continue only when it is effective.

Firstly, aid can improve the lives of millions of people. Money from rich countries can build schools, hospitals and roads, and these things helps poor communities to develop. For example, a new clinic in a village can save the lives of mothers and babies, and a road can help farmers to sell their food in the city. Aid can also pay for teachers and books, which give children a better future. Many poor countries depend of foreign aid, and without this help, many people will continue to live in poverty for many years.

Secondly, problems in poor countries can affect rich countries too. Diseases spread across borders, and wars and poverty can push people to leave their homes and look for a better life abroad. In addition, many rich nations became wealthy partly through trade with these regions, so they have a duty to give something back. However, some aid is wasted by corrupt officials, so governments should check how the money are spent and stop support if it disappears. For these reasons, rich countries cannot simply ignore what happens in poorer regions, even when their own citizens are struggling.

In conclusion, I agree that rich countries should continue to give aid during difficult times, because it saves lives and prevents problems from spreading. However, the money must be managed properly and spent on projects that really help ordinary people.

referenceAnswers.text:
Wealthy nations are regularly asked to fund clinics, schools and food programmes abroad, and some argue that this support should continue even when their own economies are weak. I agree only in part. Aid should be maintained where it is effective, but domestic hardship and corruption both justify conditions and limits.

There are strong reasons to keep aid flowing during downturns. Disease, conflict and forced migration do not stop at borders, so instability abroad eventually reaches donor countries through trade disruption, security costs and refugee flows. Aid also carries moral weight, since many rich economies grew through trade arrangements that left poorer regions dependent on exporting raw materials. Cutting support at the first sign of domestic difficulty would be both short-sighted and unjust. In this sense, aid is an investment in stability rather than a gift, and it is far cheaper than responding to a crisis later.

Conditions, however, are essential. Aid is sometimes lost to corruption or absorbed by unfinished projects, and taxpayers in a struggling economy will not accept money disappearing into accounts they cannot see. Donors should therefore publish results, fund local organisations directly and suspend payments where audits fail. Payments can also be linked to measurable results, such as the number of children vaccinated. Domestic needs also matter, since hospitals and schools at home cannot be neglected indefinitely. Aid that is transparent and effective deserves protection. Aid that is wasted does not, and with such safeguards public support is more likely to survive.

In conclusion, I agree that wealthy countries should maintain effective aid even in hard times, because the consequences of poverty cross borders, but transparent conditions are necessary and taxpayers deserve to see where their money goes.

referenceAnswers.text:
Financial aid from wealthy countries is often the first casualty of a domestic recession, and some argue that it should be protected regardless of economic conditions at home. I largely agree, because the costs of withdrawal fall on the poorest people and because instability abroad rarely stays abroad.

The strongest argument for maintaining aid is that it addresses problems that no border can contain. Epidemics spread through travel and trade, conflict displaces families towards neighbouring regions, and failed states create space for criminal networks. Money spent on vaccination, clean water and primary schooling is therefore not charity alone but a form of long-term security. No single country can vaccinate its way out of a pandemic that spreads elsewhere. Moreover, donor countries have shaped the trading rules under which many poorer economies operate, so a continuing transfer of resources is partly a matter of fair dealing.

That case does not require donors to ignore waste. Aid has too often been captured by officials, tied to suppliers in the donor country or scattered across projects that were never completed. Recession is a reason to spend more carefully, not to stop spending. Donors can publish audits, channel funds through local organisations and shift from large construction contracts towards health and education, which reach people quickly. Domestic budgets will still need protection, but the sums involved in effective aid are small compared with the cost of a regional crisis. That is a modest price for regional stability.

In conclusion, I largely agree that wealthy countries should keep giving aid during their own downturns, provided that it is monitored, targeted and honestly reported, and that the results are visible to the taxpayers who fund it.

Climate change is one of the biggest problems in the world today. Some people argue that it is mainly a global problem which needs international agreements, while others believe that ordinary people should change their own habits. Both groups have reasons for their choice, and each side has something to offer.

Firstly, supporters of international agreements argues that emissions cross borders, so no country can solve the problem alone. A factory in one country can pollute the air of its neighbours, and the sea level rises everywhere. Moreover, only governments can sign binding targets and pay for large-scale clean energy projects such as wind farms and solar power stations. Without common rules, industries can simply move to countries with weak environmental laws, and nothing will improve. For this reason, many politicians argue that only a global agreement can really work, and countries need to share new technology with each other.

Secondly, other people believe that individuals must change their habits first. Household demand for energy, food and goods causes most emissions, so ordinary choices about transport, diet and waste add up quickly. For example, if millions of people uses public transport instead of private cars and eat less meat, the effect are very big. People can also save electricity at home by using less heating and buying fewer new products. These small actions become powerful when millions of families do them together. In addition, national policies often fail when citizens ignore them, because laws cannot force everyone to recycle or save electricity.

In conclusion, some people think that climate change should be solved by international agreements, while others believe that individual habits are the key. Both sides have reasonable arguments, and it is difficult to say which is more important.

Governments negotiate emissions targets while households decide how much energy, food and transport they consume, and debate continues over which matters more. Some place the responsibility on international agreements, while others argue that ordinary people must change their habits first. Both arguments deserve examination.

Those who emphasise global agreements point out that emissions ignore national borders. A country that cuts its own pollution still suffers if its neighbours continue to burn coal, and rising sea levels threaten coastlines everywhere. Only governments, moreover, can commit to binding targets, fund large-scale renewable energy and prevent industry from relocating to countries with weaker rules. Without a common framework, individual effort in one nation can be undermined by inaction elsewhere, which is why treaties and shared standards remain central to the response. Public money, in other words, is the only tool large enough for the scale of the task.

Supporters of individual action reply that demand, not supply, drives much of the damage. Households choose how often they fly, what they eat and how they heat their homes, and these decisions collectively determine how much fossil fuel is required. Public behaviour also decides whether green policies survive elections, since governments that raise fuel taxes without public support are soon replaced. From this perspective, personal habits are not a distraction from the problem but the foundation on which any national policy must rest. When enough consumers change their behaviour, companies are forced to respond.

In conclusion, one side stresses the treaties and funding that only governments can provide, while the other highlights the daily choices of ordinary citizens. Both arguments identify a genuine part of the problem, and neither can be dismissed.

Few issues divide opinion as sharply as who should lead on climate change. Some insist that binding international agreements are the only effective instrument, while others argue that households must change their habits before any treaty can succeed. The two positions rest on different assumptions about where emissions begin.

The case for international leadership is structural. Carbon dioxide mixes in the atmosphere regardless of where it was released, so a nation that decarbonises alone still faces the consequences of its neighbours' choices. Governments alone control electricity grids, building standards, public transport budgets and the tax signals that shape industrial behaviour. They can also prevent firms from escaping regulation by relocating, an outcome that uncoordinated national efforts cannot deliver. Treaties convert scattered good intentions into enforceable obligations. Individual households cannot build a national grid or negotiate a treaty, however conscientious they may be.

The case for individual change is equally grounded. Emissions are ultimately generated by demand, and demand is created by millions of households deciding how to travel, what to eat and how warm to keep their homes. Policies that lack public consent rarely last, as fuel tax protests have shown in several countries, and consumers who adopt low-carbon habits create the market that makes clean technology affordable. Personal choices also influence those around us, spreading new norms faster than legislation can. Every solar panel installed and every journey avoided sends a signal that markets and governments eventually follow.

In conclusion, international agreements supply the rules and investment that no individual can provide, while personal habits supply the demand and political consent that make those rules work. The debate concerns emphasis rather than the facts.

Many people now get their news from websites and social media, while others prefer newspapers, radio and television because they trust them more. Both groups have good reasons for their choice, and each side has something important to offer its readers. This difference of opinion has become more common as technology changes.

Firstly, online news is fast, free and available everywhere. People can read about an event on their phone only a few minutes after it happens, and they do not have to pay for a newspaper. In addition, many different outlets and eyewitness accounts can spread the informations very quickly, and readers can compare several sources instead of trusting one editor. For example, a video recorded by a person on the street can show what really happened before journalists arrive. News websites also update their stories during the day, so readers can follow a situation as it develops.

Secondly, supporters of traditional media believe that professional editors check facts and correct errors before publication. Named journalists and publishers can be held responsible for what they print, so they are more careful than anonymous accounts online. In contrast, algorithms spread unverified stories because they attract clicks, and online news have more errors than professional reporting. Television and radio also employ many reporters in different countries, and these reporters can explain the background of a story. This kind of work costs money, but it produces more reliable information. For these reasons, less people trust social media posts, and many still prefer newspapers and television.

In conclusion, online news offers speed, low cost and many different voices, while traditional media offers careful checking and legal responsibility. Both forms of news have clear strengths, and readers often use a mixture of the two.

referenceAnswers.text:
Readers today can choose between instant updates on their phones and the slower reporting of newspapers and broadcasters, and opinions differ about which is more trustworthy. Those who rely on online sources emphasise speed and variety, while others defend the checks and accountability of established media. Both cases are worth weighing.

Online news appeals because it is immediate, free and accessible anywhere. A breaking story can reach readers within minutes, often through eyewitness footage that professional crews would take hours to match. Readers can also consult several outlets and compare how each frames the same event, rather than accepting a single editorial line. For people in regions with restricted media, social platforms may be the only available source, which makes their openness genuinely valuable. Live blogs and social feeds also allow readers to follow events as they unfold, which is impossible with a daily paper.

Traditional media, by contrast, rests on procedures that online platforms rarely match. Editors verify claims before publication, correct mistakes openly, and attach a named journalist to each report, which creates accountability and legal exposure if the story is wrong. Publishers also maintain bureaux and correspondents whose work depends on long-term credibility rather than clicks. On social platforms, by contrast, algorithms reward whatever provokes a reaction, so unverified stories often travel faster than corrections can follow. Corrections, retractions and right-of-reply procedures are slow, but they exist, and their existence shapes how carefully reporters work.

In conclusion, online sources win on speed, cost and variety, while established media offer verification and accountability. Readers who value different things will reasonably prefer different sources, and many people in practice use both.

The shift of news consumption to phones and social platforms has unsettled the assumption that professional newsrooms are the gatekeepers of reliable information. Some see this as liberation from editorial control, while others regard traditional outlets as the only dependable source. Each claim reflects a real feature of how information now travels.

Online reporting has genuine advantages. Distribution costs have collapsed, so a local protest or a distant disaster can be documented and shared within minutes by people who are actually present. Aggregation allows readers to assemble their own picture from multiple outlets, and stories that established media once ignored can reach a wide audience. In countries where the press is controlled, this openness is often the only route to independent information, and it has exposed abuses that official channels would have buried. Speed matters most when a story affects safety, such as a flood or a transport accident.

Traditional media, however, supplies something that speed cannot replace, namely verifiable accountability. A newspaper that publishes a false allegation can be sued, must print a correction and risks the reputation of named journalists. Broadcasters operate under editorial guidelines and regulatory scrutiny. Platforms, by contrast, host content without taking responsibility for its accuracy, and their recommendation systems reward emotional engagement, so fabricated stories can outrun the corrections that follow. The two models therefore reward different behaviour, and only one of them punishes error. Trust, in other words, is manufactured by institutions rather than by technology.

In conclusion, online news provides immediacy, breadth and a voice to the unheard, while traditional media offers verification and enforceable responsibility. A reader who wants both speed and accuracy must use each with an awareness of its limits.

In addition, grandparents often provides reliable childcare for working parents, which saves money and gives children emotional stability. Secondly, other people argue that old advice can be misleading. Technology, medicine and careers have changed so quickly that the experience of fifty years ago may not help a young person today. Traditional expectations about gender or marriage can also clash with modern life, and some grandparents has little knowledge of the internet or the modern job market. For these reasons, some families prefer to rely on parents and teachers instead. Parents must decide which advice is useful and which is not.

In conclusion, grandparents can pass on traditions, practical skills and emotional support, but some of their advice may be out of date. Both sides of this argument have clear reasons, and most families experience both the benefits and the problems.

Grandparents often help to raise their grandchildren, and opinions differ about how much their experience is worth. Some families value the traditions and practical knowledge that older relatives pass on, while others believe that their advice belongs to a vanished world. Both positions have merit.

Those who value grandparental influence point to the knowledge that schools and parents cannot easily supply. Family history, religious customs, recipes, crafts and stories are preserved through personal contact rather than textbooks, and a child who learns them gains a sense of belonging. Grandparents also offer practical support, collecting children from school, caring for them during illness and providing the stability that working parents need. Perhaps most importantly, regular contact with older people teaches patience, empathy and respect for a generation whose lives were very different.

The opposing view rests on the speed of modern change. Careers, technology and social expectations have shifted within a single generation, so advice that was sound in 1980 may be actively misleading today. A grandfather who never applied for a job online cannot guide a teenager through digital recruitment, and traditional views about gender roles or marriage can create conflict rather than comfort. Some older relatives also lack knowledge of mental health, modern education or the pressures of social media. Their experience is real, but it does not always transfer to present circumstances. Whether that matters depends on the family.

In conclusion, one side emphasises the traditions, practical help and emotional stability that older relatives provide, while the other questions how far their experience still applies. Both views reflect genuine family situations, and both can be true in the same household.

Within families, grandparents are the custodians of history and practical wisdom, yet their authority is questioned in a society that changes faster than any previous generation. Some argue that their knowledge remains invaluable, while others treat it as a relic. The disagreement is about whether experience keeps its value when circumstances change.

The case for continuity is substantial. Grandparents transmit what institutions cannot, including family stories, religious practice, crafts, recipes and the habits that hold a family together. They also provide childcare that is both affordable and emotionally secure, allowing parents to work while children remain within a trusted circle. Contact across generations builds patience and empathy in children, and it gives older people a purpose that improves their own health. That combination of memory and daily help is difficult to replace. In this reading, grandparents are a living archive and a practical support system at once.

The case for scepticism is equally real. Knowledge is context-bound, and advice shaped by a world of secure manufacturing jobs, early marriage and limited technology may mislead rather than guide. A grandmother who never worked outside the home cannot advise a granddaughter on negotiating a salary, and old assumptions about gender or discipline can damage relationships. Where older relatives dismiss mental health or digital careers, their influence becomes a source of conflict. The value of their experience depends heavily on whether they are willing to update it. Adaptation, rather than age, decides whether the advice still helps.

In conclusion, grandparents offer irreplaceable traditions, childcare and emotional continuity, but the usefulness of their advice varies with the subject and their willingness to adapt. Both views therefore capture part of the reality.

Climate change is a serious problem for every country. Some people argue that governments and international agreements must lead the response, while others believe that individuals should change their habits first. In my opinion, governments have the most important role, because they can change the rules for everyone.

Firstly, governments control energy supply, infrastructure and public money, so they can make big changes quickly. Only a government can build a new railway, support solar power or close a coal mine, and these decisions affect millions of people at the same time. International agreements are also important, because they stop industries from moving to countries with weaker laws. For example, when many countries agrees on the same targets, companies cannot escape regulation by moving their factories abroad. This is why government action is so powerful. Companies also follow these rules, so the effect is much bigger than any single family's effort.

Secondly, individual habits also matter, and some people say that personal choices are the fastest way to reduce emissions. Families can fly less, drive less and waste less food, and these changes have an immediate effect. However, individuals cannot choose the electricity that arrives at their homes or the buses that run in their cities, so their choices are limited by the systems around them. In my view, personal action supports government policy but cannot replace it, because one person alone cannot change the national grid. This is why I believe government action must come first.

In conclusion, I believe that governments and international agreements must lead the fight against climate change, because only they can change energy systems and rules. Individual habits are helpful but not enough on their own.

Emissions continue to rise despite decades of warnings, and the argument over who should act first has become sharper. Some insist that governments and international agreements must lead, while others argue that individuals should change their habits immediately. In my opinion, government leadership is essential, though individual behaviour determines whether it succeeds.

Governments possess the instruments that match the scale of the problem. They set building standards, fund public transport, price carbon and negotiate the treaties that prevent industry from relocating to avoid regulation. A single decision to close coal plants or to subsidise electric vehicles can cut emissions more than millions of household choices combined. Individuals cannot construct a power grid or sign an international agreement, so expecting personal action to carry the burden is unrealistic. This is not a matter of individual willpower but of the options that are available. Private households, by contrast, cannot rewrite building regulations or national energy policy.

Individual habits are not irrelevant. Demand created by households shapes what companies produce, and public opinion decides whether ambitious policies survive at the ballot box. Governments that raise fuel taxes without public support have repeatedly been forced to retreat. In my view, personal choices are most valuable as political pressure, because a citizen who cycles, recycles and votes for green policies reinforces the very measures that make those choices easier for everyone else. Every consumer who installs insulation or takes the train reduces demand for fossil fuel directly, and these choices also normalise new behaviour among friends and neighbours.

In conclusion, I believe that governments and international agreements must lead, because only they can change infrastructure and law at the necessary scale, while individual habits provide the demand and consent that make those changes durable.

The response to climate change is often framed as a choice between government treaties and household habits. Some argue that only coordinated state action can matter, while others insist that change begins with individuals. I believe governments must lead, because the levers that determine emissions are concentrated in their hands.

The decisive argument for state leadership is structural. Emissions are produced by energy systems, transport networks, buildings and industry, and these are shaped by regulation, taxation and public investment rather than by consumer preference alone. A household cannot choose a cleaner national grid, and a commuter cannot create a bus route. When a government prices carbon, mandates efficiency standards or funds rail links, it alters the options available to millions of people simultaneously, which no campaign of personal virtue can replicate. The choice facing a commuter is created by previous public decisions.

Individual behaviour nonetheless determines how far such policies can travel. Households that reduce flying, meat consumption and waste create immediate reductions, and their choices signal demand for cleaner products. More importantly, citizens decide whether governments stay in office, and policies that lack public consent are frequently reversed, as fuel tax protests in several countries have demonstrated. Yet personal action operates within a framework that only states can build, which is why it reinforces leadership rather than replacing it. Leadership and personal responsibility are therefore complements rather than rivals. Neither can deliver alone.

In conclusion, I believe governments and international agreements must lead the response, because energy, transport and industry can only be transformed at scale by law and public investment, while individual habits provide the support that makes such transformation politically sustainable.

International tourism has grown quickly in recent years. Some people believe that it brings clear benefits to local communities, while others argue that it damages local culture and daily life. In my opinion, tourism help local people more than it harms them.

Firstly, visitor spending creates jobs in hotels, guiding, food and crafts. In many towns, tourism is the main source of income, and families depend of the money that visitors leave behind. Tourist income can also pay for the repair of historic buildings and for new roads and airports. Hotels, restaurants and shops also buy food and products from local farmers, so the money spreads through the whole town. This income matters most in areas where farming or fishing alone cannot support every family. In addition, contact between visitors and residents builds understanding and language skills, because local people practise English and learn about other countries.

Secondly, however, tourism can cause serious problems. Seasonal, low-paid work creates less jobs than people expect, and profits often leaves the region instead of staying with local families. Festivals and crafts can become staged performances for paying visitors, so traditions lose their meaning. Rising rents and crowded public spaces can also push residents away from the centre of their own towns. Many young people leave their hometowns to work in other cities when tourism jobs are poorly paid. For these reasons, some communities feel that tourism has damaged their way of life.

In conclusion, I believe that international tourism brings more benefits than damage, because it creates jobs and income. However, governments must manage it carefully so that local culture is protected and local people can decide how their towns develop.

Tourism has become a pillar of many local economies, and its effects are debated wherever visitors arrive in force. Some see clear benefits for host communities, while others point to damaged traditions and disrupted daily life. In my opinion, the benefits outweigh the costs, provided that growth is managed rather than encouraged.

The economic case is straightforward. Visitor spending sustains hotels, restaurants, guides, drivers and craft workshops, and in regions with few other industries it is often the only source of employment. Entry fees and taxes paid by tourists can finance the restoration of historic buildings, museums and national parks that would otherwise decay. Hotels and restaurants also buy vegetables, meat and craft products from nearby farms, so visitor spending circulates through the whole community. Contact with visitors also builds language skills and cultural confidence, since residents explain their traditions to outsiders and see them valued.

The damage, however, is real. Work in tourism is frequently seasonal and low-paid, and profits often flow to foreign tour operators rather than staying in the community. Festivals may be shortened or staged for paying audiences, and craft traditions can be reduced to souvenirs. Rising rents, crowded streets and water shortages push residents out of the very districts that visitors come to see. Local people may also lose access to beaches, markets and temples that visitors now dominate. These problems are serious, yet they reflect poor management rather than tourism itself.

In conclusion, I believe that international tourism brings greater benefits than harm, because it provides income and preserves heritage, but only when local communities control how it develops and are able to limit visitor numbers.

International tourism is described both as a lifeline for local communities and as a threat to their way of life. Both claims can be true, but the balance depends on who owns it. In my view, tourism benefits communities only when local people retain control, and often that condition is not met.

Where tourism is locally owned, its benefits are undeniable. Family-run guesthouses, guides and food producers capture visitor spending directly, and the income supports schools, clinics and the upkeep of historic sites. Cultural contact can also strengthen pride in local traditions, since crafts and festivals acquire value in the eyes of outsiders as well as residents. Tourism of this kind diversifies an economy that may previously have depended on a single crop or industry. A village that runs its own tours keeps the income, the decision-making and the pride that comes with both.

Ownership, however, is often external. International tour operators, hotel chains and absentee landlords capture much of the revenue, while residents supply seasonal labour at low wages. The consequences extend beyond income. Rents rise as apartments are converted for visitors, public spaces fill with crowds, and festivals are compressed into performances for paying audiences. Residents then find themselves priced out of the neighbourhoods their culture made attractive in the first place. Without local control, the costs of tourism are concentrated in the community while the profits leave it. Tourism then becomes an extraction industry rather than a partnership.

In conclusion, I believe international tourism can strengthen local communities, but only when residents own and direct it. Otherwise its cultural and social costs tend to outweigh the income it brings, and residents are left with the crowd but not the profit.

In cities where flats are small, a local park works like an extra garden for thousands of residents, and it costs far less than a new hospital or sports centre. Residents who live near a park also tend to walk more and feel less stress, which reduces pressure on health services.

Secondly, however, a shortage of homes pushes up rents and increases homelessness. When there is not enough flats, young people cannot afford to live near their jobs, and workers travel long distances every day. People also need to live close to schools, hospitals and workplaces, so new housing in the city centre is more useful than housing on the edge. The amount of homes is the main problem, and small green areas between buildings can still be added, so the city does not need to choose between homes and parks completely. Families are smaller than in the past, so more homes are needed.

In conclusion, I believe that building homes should come first in crowded cities, because people needs somewhere to live, but planners should include small parks in every new development so that residents have both a home and somewhere to relax.

As cities grow, undeveloped land becomes contested, and planners must weigh housing against open space. Some argue that parks should be protected, while others insist that homes must come first. In my opinion, housing deserves priority in most cases, but only if green space is guaranteed within each new development.

The case for housing is difficult to dismiss. A shortage of homes raises rents, forces young workers to commute long distances and increases homelessness, and these problems affect the poorest residents first. People also need to live near their jobs, schools and hospitals, since long journeys cost money and damage family life. Brownfield sites and empty offices can be converted, but in successful cities demand consistently outruns supply, so new construction is unavoidable. In many successful cities, workers in essential jobs can no longer afford to live within an hour of their workplace, which damages both families and public services.

The case for open space is equally serious. Parks and street trees cool dense neighbourhoods, absorb pollution and give children somewhere to play, and residents of small flats rely on them as an extension of their homes. Green areas also bring neighbours together and reduce the isolation that high-rise living can create. Once a park is built over, the land is effectively lost for a century or more. The sensible answer is not to choose between the two but to build more compactly, with courtyards, roof gardens and small squares included in every new district.

In conclusion, I believe that building homes should come first in crowded cities, but the open space that makes those homes liveable must be planned into the development rather than added later.

In dense cities, land is the scarcest resource, and decisions about it shape whom the city serves. Some argue that open space must be protected, while others insist homes take priority. I believe open space should be defended, because housing can be built upward, whereas a park, once lost, is rarely recovered.

The argument for protecting green space rests on what it does for a dense population. Trees and parks lower street temperatures, absorb air pollution and give children a safe place to play, functions that no building can perform. In neighbourhoods of small flats, public open space effectively enlarges every home, and it brings together residents who would otherwise never meet. These benefits are also permanent in a way that housing is not, since a park serves every generation while a poorly located tower block may be obsolete within decades. A mature tree takes decades to replace, if it can be replaced at all.

The demand for housing is nonetheless urgent and cannot be dismissed. Rising rents displace long-standing communities and push essential workers far from the centre, and homelessness is a visible failure of supply. Yet the choice is not as stark as it appears. Cities can build upward on existing sites, convert empty offices, and require courtyards or roof gardens in new schemes. Density, in other words, is the answer to both needs at once. What cannot be replaced is a mature park, because once land is covered by concrete, the trees, soil and public memory of that space are gone.

In conclusion, I believe cities should protect their open space and meet housing need through density, conversion and better design, because parks serve everyone permanently while building sites can be found elsewhere.

More and more employees are leaving their jobs to work for themselves instead of for a company. This trend has become common in many countries. There are clear advantages, such as freedom, but there are also disadvantages, such as a less secure income.

The main advantage is control over working hours, projects and clients. A self-employed person can decide when to start work, which tasks to accept and how much to charge, and this freedom is impossible in most companies. There is also no fixed salary ceiling if the business grows, so successful owners can earn much more than employees in the same industry. In addition, the work can be done from any location, which mean that parents or students can fit their jobs around other responsibilities. This flexibility is one reason why the number of self-employed parents has grown so quickly.

However, there are serious disadvantages. Self-employed workers has no paid holiday, sick pay or pension, so illness or a quiet month can cause real financial problems. Their income is irregular, and many owners takes on personal debt when the business is slow. They also handle tax, insurance, equipment and the search for new clients themselves, which takes many unpaid hours. Health insurance and pension contributions must also be paid from their own pocket, which reduces the real value of their earnings. If the business fails, the owner may lose savings as well as income. For these reasons, self-employment is not suitable for everyone.

In conclusion, working for yourself offers freedom, higher earnings and flexible locations, but it also brings financial risk and a heavy workload. People should consider both sides before they leave a permanent job, and there is no single answer that suits everybody.

A growing number of employees are leaving permanent positions to work for themselves, and this shift is changing how people think about careers. Self-employment offers genuine rewards, but it also transfers risks from the employer to the individual. Both sides deserve careful consideration, since the decision affects more than income.

The advantages begin with autonomy. Independent workers choose their own hours, clients and projects, which makes it easier to combine work with family responsibilities or study. Successful businesses also remove the salary ceiling that limits employees, and ownership means that every improvement in the business benefits the person who built it. Freedom of location is a further attraction, since most freelance work can be delivered from anywhere with a reliable internet connection. The work can also be chosen to match personal interests, which is rare in a salaried role. For many people, this alignment of work and values is worth more than a secure contract.

The disadvantages are equally practical. Self-employed people receive no paid holiday, sick pay or employer pension contribution, so a single illness can erase months of savings. Income fluctuates with demand, and slow periods often force owners into personal debt. Administrative duties also consume unpaid hours, because tax returns, insurance and the search for clients all fall on the owner. Savings are also needed to cover quiet periods, which many new freelancers underestimate. The result is that independence demands discipline as well as ambition. The freedom that makes self-employment attractive therefore carries costs that employees rarely see.

In conclusion, self-employment offers autonomy, unlimited earnings and flexibility, while it demands financial resilience and administrative work. The choice depends on how much security an individual is willing to exchange for independence, and on the savings they have.

Independence brings rewards that salaried positions rarely match, yet it also exposes individuals to risks that employers once absorbed. The advantages and disadvantages are therefore two sides of the same decision.

The advantages centre on ownership and control. Self-employed workers decide which projects to accept, when to work and where to live, and these choices allow them to build careers around family, health or study. Income is not capped by a salary scale, so a successful consultancy or craft business can earn far more than the same skills would command in employment. Ownership also means that effort and reward are directly linked, which many people find more motivating than a fixed wage. Independent work also builds a portfolio of clients and projects that belongs to the worker rather than to an employer.

The disadvantages are structural rather than accidental. An employee's contract includes paid leave, sick pay, pension contributions and equipment, and all of these become the individual's responsibility once they work alone. Revenue is unpredictable, so a slow quarter can turn into personal debt, and administrative tasks such as tax, insurance and client acquisition consume hours that generate no income. Illness or burnout, which an employer would absorb, can end a small business entirely. Even a short hospital stay can halt income completely, because there is no colleague to cover the work.

In conclusion, self-employment delivers autonomy, uncapped earnings and locational freedom, but it replaces the security of a contract with personal financial risk and unpaid administration. The trade-off is real on both sides and deserves careful thought.

The main advantage is that a whole library fits into one light device. Text size, brightness and search functions can also be adjusted, which helps older readers and people with poor eyesight. For travellers and students, these features makes reading much easier. A single device can also store textbooks, novels and newspapers together, so readers always have something to read.

However, there are disadvantages too. Long screen sessions tire the eyes and can disturb sleep, especially when people read on their phones late at night. Some readers also remembers less of what they read on a screen, because it is easy to move quickly and lose concentration. In addition, digital files depend on batteries, accounts and platforms that may not last, and a printed book can still be read when the electricity fails. For deep reading, many people still choose print rather than a glowing screen. For these reasons, some people prefers paper.

In conclusion, digital reading offers portability, low prices and adjustable text, while it can harm sleep, reduce concentration and depend on technology. Both formats have clear strengths, and most readers use a mixture of them. The best choice depends on the situation.
